The central question is: how stale can a feature vector be before a recommendation model's predictions degrade past an acceptable loss threshold — and how do you set that tolerance dynamically when the underlying data distribution is itself shifting? In a real-time recommendation pipeline, features like user click recency, item popularity decay, and session context have wildly different temporal half-lives — a user's last-click embedding might be valid for minutes while a trending-item score expires in seconds — so a single global TTL on the feature store is almost always wrong. Concept drift compounds this: when user behavior shifts (seasonal patterns, viral events, platform redesign), the joint distribution P(y | x) changes, meaning a feature vector that was predictively valid yesterday carries a different signal today even if the values themselves haven't changed. The naive engineering fix — just lower all TTLs aggressively — creates a different failure mode: cache miss storms that overload upstream feature computation, forcing the pipeline into fallback paths (often population-mean imputations) that are more stale and less personalized than the slightly-expired cached value would have been.

What a beginner misses is that staleness tolerance is not a property of the feature in isolation but of the feature × model × distribution triplet: a gradient-boosted tree trained on dense historical data may be far more robust to a stale popularity score than a two-tower neural retrieval model whose embedding dot-products are calibrated to a tight recency window, so the same 5-minute-old feature can be harmless in one model and catastrophically misleading in another. Experts also worry about drift detection latency asymmetry — the window between when drift begins and when your monitoring system fires an alert is precisely the window during which your staleness thresholds are wrong and you don't know it.

The decision boundary is fundamentally a latency budget arbitrage: route around the feature store when the cost of a cache miss (recompute latency) is lower than the cost of serving a stale feature (revenue-weighted CTR degradation), and you can only know this if you've instrumented both sides — Doordash's 2022 ML platform writeup describes exactly this tradeoff in their ETA feature pipeline, where inline recomputation of certain geo-temporal features at p99 added ~8ms but recovered measurable order conversion versus serving 90-second-old store values during demand surges. The routing decision boundary needs to encode three costs simultaneously: recompute latency (p99, not mean, because tail latency kills recommendation throughput), upstream system load (inline recompute during a traffic spike may cascade into the very systems causing the drift), and feature importance weight from the current model (a high-drift but low-weight feature doesn't justify inline recompute at all). The critical constraint is that parameter updates within a fixed functional form are always safer than structural mutations: systems like Google's Feature Store (described in the Vertex AI documentation) allow "warm" parameter updates — pushing new normalization statistics, updated vocabulary mappings, or revised bucketization boundaries — without versioning the transformation graph, because the model's learned weights remain valid as long as the transformation's output schema and monotonic ordering properties are preserved. For structural mutations that genuinely require covariance adjustment without full retraining, the emerging practice is adapter layers: freeze the base model, insert a thin learned projection (1-2 linear layers) between the mutated feature and the model's original input layer, and train only the adapter on recent streaming data — this is analogous to LoRA in LLM fine-tuning and can converge on hours of online data rather than requiring a full offline retrain cycle. The expert worry here is mutation ordering under concurrent drift: if multiple features are simultaneously drifting and their transformations are being mutated on different schedules, the covariance structure is in a perpetual intermediate state that neither the original model nor any single patched version was trained on, and the only rigorous solution is to gate all mutations through a single atomic commit that shadow-validates the joint transformed feature vector, not individual features in isolation.

The subtle expert concern is label delay confounding: in recommendation systems, conversion labels (purchases, long-dwell clicks) arrive with latency of minutes to hours, so the adapter's "online" loss is computed on impression-level proxy labels (immediate clicks) that may have a different drift profile than the true optimization target — an adapter that appears converged on proxy labels may be silently diverging on delayed true labels, requiring a parallel evaluation path that waits for label materialization before updating divergence status. The foundational architectural requirement is serving-time snapshot logging: every inference must log not just the request and response but the exact adapter weights checkpoint ID and feature vector that produced it, stored in an immutable event ledger (Kafka with infinite retention or an S3-backed log compaction layer) so that when delayed labels arrive hours later, you can reconstruct precisely which model state generated each prediction — without this, retroactive correction is impossible because you can't distinguish whether a misprediction came from a bad adapter update or a stale feature. The attribution problem in deep embedding models is fundamentally an influence localization problem, and the tractable approximation is to work in gradient subspaces defined by the input embedding layer rather than the full parameter space: since a feature's influence must flow through its embedding lookup before diffusing into deeper layers, you can localize conflict detection to the embedding table rows corresponding to that feature's vocabulary entries — this is approximate but captures the first-order parameter subspace most directly affected, and systems like Meta's DLRM architecture make this natural because embedding tables are already partitioned by feature ID. The computationally feasible production implementation is per-feature gradient checksum comparison: rather than tracking full gradient vectors per parameter, maintain a low-dimensional sketch (e.g., a random projection of the gradient vector into R^512) separately for each stream, then compute cosine similarity in the sketched space — this gives an approximate conflict signal at O(512) cost per feature per batch rather than O(parameters), and the Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma guarantees that cosine similarity is preserved within epsilon with high probability for sufficiently large sketch dimension.
